summary: Explains how RFC authors should write the IANA Considerations section. Many protocols have fields whose values must be assigned without clashing, and IANA keeps those registries. This document defines a framework for stating the policies under which new values may be added or changed. It replaces RFC 5226.

eli5.summary: Think of a school locker room with numbered lockers. This is the rule book for how new lockers get handed out, so two kids never get the same one.

subtitle: How to write an IANA Considerations section and choose the rules for handing out protocol numbers and names.

tldr.problem: Protocols use constants such as codes and names that must not clash, and someone has to coordinate who gets which value and under what rules.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8126 sets out what a document must say when it creates a registry or asks for values in one, defines ten well-known registration policies, and describes the role of designated experts.
tldr.outcome: Authors get a shared vocabulary and checklist for clear instructions to IANA. It obsoletes RFC 5226 and is updated by RFC 9907.

facts.label: Expert response time
facts.value: A week for simple requests to a few weeks for complex ones

sections.title: Namespaces, Registries and the IANA Considerations Section
sections.content:
Many protocols have points of extensibility that use constants to identify parameters. To keep those values from conflicting, allocation is often coordinated by a central record keeper, a role that IANA fills for IETF protocols. The RFC calls the range of possible values a namespace, binding a value to a purpose an assignment or registration, and the place where this is recorded a registry. The Protocol field in the IP header and MIME media types are its examples.

Guidance on when values are assigned is normally written in a dedicated section titled "IANA Considerations". That section should collect clear, concise instructions for IANA, while technical documentation lives elsewhere and is only referenced. An ideal section lists each requested action, gives full registry names and points to the rest of the document. Requests are phrased to IANA ("IANA is asked to assign..."), and the RFC Editor later changes them to say what was done.
sections.eli5: When many people need unique numbers, one office keeps the list. The note you give that office should be short and clear, with the long explanation kept somewhere else.

sections.title: Creating and Revising Registries
sections.content:
A document that creates a new namespace and expects IANA to maintain it must give clear instructions, either in the IANA Considerations section or referenced from it. These must include the name of the registry, the information registrants must provide, the registration policy that will apply to future requests, the size, format and syntax of entries, and any initial assignments and reservations.

Registries are anchored from the IANA Protocol Registries page, and authors should say which existing group a new registry belongs in. Strings are expected to be ASCII. The RFC also advises that every registry specify a change control policy and a change controller. For IETF-stream RFCs, change control lies by default with the IESG.

Changing an existing registry follows a process similar to creating one, with a document that refers to the existing namespace. If a new column is added, the instructions must say how to fill it for existing entries. In straightforward cases, such as adding a status column or correcting an error, the IESG may approve an update without a new document.
sections.eli5: When you start a new list, you write down its name, what each line must contain, who is allowed to add lines and who can fix them later.

sections.title: Registering Values in an Existing Registry
sections.content:
A document that asks for a value should identify the registry by its exact name as listed on the IANA web page, cite the RFC that defines it, and make clear which range is wanted if the registry has ranges with different policies. It must supply all required information and follow any special process, such as a registration template or posting to a mailing list.

Numeric values are normally chosen by IANA when the document is approved. Drafts should use placeholders such as TBD1 and TBD2, not pick their own numbers, lest IANA give one to another document in the meantime. Text strings are normally specified in the document, and a draft may use a draft-specific value such as foobar-testing-draft-05 during testing. For early implementations, a document can request early allocation (see RFC 7120).

The IESG may override registration procedures case by case where an assignment is obviously right but updating the process first is too onerous. IANA may also ask the IESG for advice when procedures are unclear or requests look unusual or abusive. Registrations that carry extra data, such as media types, may be updated by their registrants or change controllers.
sections.eli5: If you want a locker number, you ask the office by its proper name and write "number to be decided". You do not scribble a number on the locker yourself, because someone else might get it.

sections.title: The Well-Known Registration Policies
sections.content:
A registration policy controls how new assignments are accepted. The RFC advises choosing the least strict policy that fits the registry, and looking for specific justification for anything stricter than Expert Review or Specification Required. Registration must not be unnecessarily difficult, costly or subject to denial, because a registry that does not reflect what is in use is devalued. Ten policies are defined for common use: Private Use, Experimental Use, Hierarchical Allocation, First Come First Served, Expert Review, Specification Required, RFC Required, IETF Review, Standards Action and IESG Approval.

Private Use and Experimental Use are not recorded by IANA at all. Hierarchical Allocation delegates part of the namespace, as with DNS top-level domains. IESG Approval is a rarely used fall-back for when another mechanism cannot be used in time.

From First Come First Served to Standards Action the policies run in increasing strictness. Registries can combine them, for example IETF Review for requests in IETF documents and Specification Required for requests from outside standards bodies. Provisional registrations, which are more readily changed or removed, are also described.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to hand out lockers: anyone who asks gets the next one, or a teacher must check first, or the whole school council must agree. Stricter ways are used only for things that are scarce or risky.

sections.title: Designated Experts
sections.content:
Some policies, Expert Review and Specification Required, rely on a designated expert: an individual who evaluates a request and returns a recommendation to IANA. IANA cannot follow every mailing list discussion or judge whether it has reached consensus, so it delegates the question of whether to assign a value. Experts are generally not meant to be gatekeepers, and should check for completeness, interoperability and conflicts with existing protocols and options.

For registries created by the IETF, the IESG appoints experts, normally on the recommendation of the relevant Area Director. Experts must respond in a timely fashion, normally within a week for simple requests to a few weeks for complex ones. If no documented criteria exist, the presumption should be that a code point is granted unless there is a compelling reason against, such as scarcity of code points, unclear documentation, or an extension that would harm existing systems. An expert with a conflict of interest should recuse himself. Documents must not name the experts in the document itself.
sections.eli5: A designated expert is like a helpful librarian who checks whether a new book belongs on the shelf and tells the office yes or no, and must be able to explain why.

sections.title: Status Labels and Registry References
sections.content:
The RFC defines well-known labels for an assignment or range: Private Use, Experimental, Unassigned, Reserved and Known Unregistered Use. Unassigned and Reserved are distinctly different: unassigned values can be assigned through documented procedures, while reserved values are held back for special uses and are not available.

References in a registry should point implementors to the document that defines and explains the item, not merely to the document that performs the registration, and should include section numbers where useful. The RFC also covers closing a registry, so no new registrations are accepted while existing ones stay valid, and marking entries as obsolete or deprecated.
sections.eli5: A locker can be free, saved for later, or open for anyone to borrow without writing it down. Each label tells people what they may do with it.

sections.title: Revised Documents and Reclaiming Values
sections.content:
When a "bis" document obsoletes an earlier RFC that created registries or registered entries, registrations that reference the old document should usually be updated to point to the current one. The IANA Considerations of the new document can either list specific changes or ask IANA to change every reference to the old RFC to the new one. Entries no longer in use may keep pointing to the old document.

Documents with no IANA actions should still include an IANA Considerations section that says "This document has no IANA actions." Reclaiming assigned values is described as tricky because deployed systems may still use them. It should involve contacting the original party, normally needs the original requester's concurrence, and requires IESG Approval when done against objection.
sections.eli5: When a new edition of a rule book replaces an old one, the index must point to the new edition, and a note saying "nothing to do here" is better than leaving a page out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Information that creates or updates a registration needs to be authenticated and authorized. IANA updates registries according to instructions in published RFCs and from the IESG, and may also accept clarifications from authors, working group chairs, designated experts and mailing list participants.

Security must be considered when choosing a registration policy, because registering some parameters has security implications and needs suitable review. New vulnerabilities may need to be attached to existing registrations so users are not misled about the security of a registered number.
sections.eli5: Only the right people should be allowed to change the list, and if a locker turns out to be unsafe, a warning should be written next to it.

Approval by a designated expert, with enough information to evaluate.
Expert approval plus a permanent, readily available public specification.
Publication in an RFC from any stream.
An RFC in the IETF Stream with IETF consensus.
A Standards Track or BCP RFC in the IETF Stream.
